thread:
maria: Quick RFC follow-up — proposal to add resource-scoped API keys (project+resource) instead of only org-scoped keys. thinking about migration path + runtime check perf. :thinking:

josh: curious about the runtime cost — do we plan a DB lookup per request? that will add tail latency for small requests.

sam: we could embed a signed scope claim in the key (short, HMAC) and validate locally, fallback to lookup only for revocation/audit. avoids per-request DB hits.

maria: exactly. two modes: 1) self-contained token (signed claims, TTL) 2) opaque token -> lookup. clients pick tradeoff.

leah: legacy keys are opaque today. migration pain: many customers use long-lived keys in CI. how to rotate transparently?

rachel: plan idea: issue new resource-scoped keys alongside old keys; accept both for 6 months; emit deprecation log and default new SDKs to new keys. also add "scope-info" endpoint to validate without performing action.

josh: +1 but we need to consider RBAC mapping complexity: resources can inherit project permissions, but we also allow per-resource overrides. policy evaluation could blow up.

sam: suggestion: keep RBAC separate from token scope. token only says what resource(s) it grants; policy engine still checks subject->role bindings. token narrows target resources for fast allow/deny path. i.e., token scope := candidate set, policy eval intersects with bindings.

maria: behavior detail: if token scope is empty (org) -> normal policy path. if token scope present -> check resource in token scope first; if not present, short-circuit deny. avoids expensive policy eval in deny cases.

leah: audit implications: need to preserve original principal in logs when using signed tokens (we currently log api_key_id). for self-contained tokens include "k": api_key_id claim so auditors can tie events back.

rachel: example token payload we discussed: ```{ "k":"ak_1234","s":["proj:42","proj:42/res:model-abc"],"exp":1718690000,"sig":"..." }``` use compact base64 + dot format like: ak.b64payload.sig

josh: what about revocation? signed tokens can't be revoked without server-side blacklist. we can use short TTL (hours) and maintain ephemeral revoke list for exceptions.

sam: agreed. TTL of 4h for most, 24h for special long-lived after approval. add revocation cache checked only on misses or admin flagged keys to reduce checks.

maria: migration checklist draft: 1) issue new keys in console + SDK helpers 2) accept both token types server-side 3) add logs + telemetry to measure usage 4) phase out opaque after 6-12 months 5) provide rotation CLI for customers

leah: can we support a token-exchange flow for CI where customers swap long-lived opaque -> short-lived signed with a single call? reduces friction.

rachel: yep, implement an exchange endpoint that requires org admin and logs the exchange. returned short-lived signed token scoped to requested project.

deploy-bot: deploy queued: auth-service:v2-resource-scope-check (canary -> 5% -> 25%) scheduled in 10m. :rocket:

josh: ok, two immediate engineering tasks: A) add local verifier for signed token (lib + security review) B) design revocation cache (memory + redis fallback).

sam: I'll prototype verifier and bench verify cost (crypto HMAC + JSON parse) against current auth path. 95th p99 goals need numbers.

maria: thanks — can we aim for a short RFC doc with the outlined migration timeline and examples? I'll draft and @eng-sre for SLO consideration. :+1:

leah: one more: SDKs must default to using the exchange flow for new keys so we don't nudge users to copy long-lived secrets into CI.

rachel: noted. I'll add SDK stories to the RFC.

maria: great thread. we'll sync in the follow-up design meeting next Tue.
